description:
Space Saviors — São Paulo, Brazil

We are four 10-year-old fifth-graders from São Paulo, plus one parent keeping us on schedule. We build a playable 3D mission-design game: choose an orbit, assemble a spacecraft, check your mass and delta-v, and launch — if the math does not close, the mission does not fly. Our four missions follow real ones (ADRAS-J2, DART, Perseverance, Europa Clipper). We cover game design, coding, mission research and testing.
summary: Space Saviors was created by a team of four 10-year-old Brazilian 5th graders and one adult in just two days. It is a free 3D browser game that teaches how real space missions are designed by allowing players to choose from the following missions: clearing space junk; deflecting asteroids; landing a rover; or exploring Europa. They pick an orbit and build a spacecraft with the following limited resources: mass, power, budget, data storage, communications and time. A Mission Control Check tells players whether the design is ready to launch, and a Mission Report details what worked or failed and why. In the Rocket Workshop, players individually assemble a rocket. In Team Mode, up to four players work together on a mission. The game uses actual NASA data (e.g. radius of Earth), so every trade-off is grounded in real physics. Each mission is linked to real ones, such as NASA's DART and ESA's ClearSpace-1 (simplifications are detailed in the Data & Credits panel). The goal is to make space engineering feel possible for everyone. Players learn by doing: designing, testing, retrying, like real engineers. Our message: space engineering is based on teamwork, math and creativity, and every choice has a trade-off. Code and graphics were made with Claude; and demo was narrated with a synthetic voice.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Space Saviors is a single-page 3D game for the Space Apps Challenge that puts players in the role of a space-mission engineer. Players tackle one of four missions—space junk removal, asteroid deflection, Mars rover placement, or Europa exploration—by choosing an orbit and selecting or building a spacecraft while balancing six resources: mass, power, budget, data storage, communications, and time. Before launch, Mission Control reviews the design. Afterward, a detailed mission report explains the outcome and the decisions that contributed to success or failure. In the Rocket Workshop, players can assemble a custom rocket using a nose cone, fairing, tank, engine, fins, boosters, and decoupler. Team mode allows two to four players to share one screen, mission, and budget; each player has a role, and everyone must agree before launch.

HOW IT WORKS

Orbit speed (v = √(GM/r)) and orbit period (T = 2π√(r³/GM)) are calculated live for the orbit the player picks. Fuel needs follow the rocket equation (delta-v = exhaust speed × ln(start mass ÷ end mass)). Each mission screen shows a "Real NASA fact" and a "Real missions" note linking the game to real spacecraft: ADRAS-J2 and ClearSpace-1 (debris removal), DART and Hera (asteroids), Curiosity and Perseverance (Mars), Europa Clipper and JUICE (Europa).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Space missions can be hard to understand because every decision affects others. The game makes these trade-offs visible and playable. Designed for families and classrooms, it helps people discover how space engineering brings together teamwork and creative problem-solving—and how much fun that can be.

NASA DATA USED

Gravity, GM and radius of Earth, Mars and Europa, and sunlight strength at Mars and Jupiter from the NASA Planetary Fact Sheet. The ideal rocket equation (NASA Glenn), orbital formulas (NASA Basics of Space Flight), and mission facts from NASA's DART, Curiosity, Europa Clipper and Orbital Debris Program Office pages. Real-mission notes also draw on ESA's Hera and ClearSpace-1 pages and Astroscale's ADRAS-J2 page. All sources are listed in the in-game "Data & Credits" panel.

Simplified for play (not real NASA engineering data): prices and the money system, part masses, power numbers, data volumes, delta-v targets, orbit bonuses and rocket lift effects. The 3D view is not to scale.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one file; three.js r149 (MIT License) for 3D; fonts Inter and Space Grotesk (Open Font License). Planets, the space station, the rocket and spacecraft are drawn by code, not photos. No NASA logos or insignia are used.

While the concept, rules, missions, economy and part prices were created by the Space Saviors team, the team developed and tested code and graphics with AI's assistance (Claude). Video and synthetic voice were also developed with AI.

CREATIVE ASPECT

Players do not just read about missions: they design, test and fail safely. Four different worlds, a build-your-own-rocket workshop and shared-screen crew roles turn engineering into a team game.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy (NASA values when available, labeled when simplified), age-appropriate language, teamwork, and safety (minors cannot be identified).
